extraction_notes.note: The theorem environment ends at 'we have the followings:'; its two conclusions sit in an {\it enumerate} after \end{theorem}. They are emitted as claims ClP4/ClP5 (outside the theorem span, so not nested), with uses edges from TP2 and proves edges from PP1.
Equation (2.1) is named 'magnetostatic Maxwell's equation'; retyped as an external theorem (physical law) rather than an equation.
Parameter settings, stopping criterion, tables of RMSE/SSIM and CPU-time comparisons in Section 3 and discursive text on artifacts are not extracted; only the headline numerical claim ClP12 is kept.

nodes.statement: Quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM) \cite{L.deRochefort2010} is a novel imaging technique that visualizes the magnetic susceptibility distribution from the measured field data associated with magnetization ${\mathbf M}=(M_1,M_2,M_3)$ induced in the body by an MR scanner.
differentia: visualizes the magnetic susceptibility distribution from the measured field data

nodes.name: Magnetic susceptibility
nodes.statement: The magnetic susceptibility $\chi$ is an intrinsic property of the material which relates ${\mathbf M}$ and the magnetic field ${\mathbf H}=(H_1,H_2,H_3)$ through ${\mathbf M}=\chi{\mathbf H}$ \cite{J.K.Seo2014}.
nodes.genus: an intrinsic property of the material
differentia: relates ${\mathbf M}$ and the magnetic field ${\mathbf H}=(H_1,H_2,H_3)$ through ${\mathbf M}=\chi{\mathbf H}$

nodes.name: Main static magnetic field
nodes.statement: More concretely, assume that an object is placed in an MR scanner with the main static magnetic field $\mathbf{B}_0=(0,0,B_0)$ where $B_0$ is a positive constant.

nodes.name: Complex GRE signal model
nodes.statement:
Then, for any $\boldsymbol{x}\in{\mathbb R}^3$, the observed complex GRE signal $I(\boldsymbol{x},TE)$ at an echo time $TE\mathrm{sec}$ is modeled as
\begin{align} I(\boldsymbol{x},TE)=m(\boldsymbol{x})\exp\left\{-i\left(b(\boldsymbol{x})\omega_0B_0TE+\theta_0(\boldsymbol{x})\right)\right\},
\end{align}
where $\omega_0=42.577 \mathrm{MHz/T}$ is the proton gyromagnetic ratio, $b$ is the total field induced by the susceptibility distribution in an MR scanner, and $\theta_0$ is the coil sensitivity dependent phase offset.
nodes.statement_short: GRE signal I = magnitude times exp of phase linear in the total field b plus a coil phase offset.

nodes.name: Complex GRE signal model
nodes.statement: I(\boldsymbol{x},TE)=m(\boldsymbol{x})\exp\left\{-i\left(b(\boldsymbol{x})\omega_0B_0TE+\theta_0(\boldsymbol{x})\right)\right\},
nodes.label: ComplexMR

nodes.name: MR phase
Phase model
nodes.statement: \theta(\boldsymbol{x})=b(\boldsymbol{x})\omega_0B_0TE+\theta_0(\boldsymbol{x}).
nodes.label: phasemodel

nodes.name: Region of interest (ROI)
nodes.statement: Based on the observations $\theta(\boldsymbol{x})$, QSM aims at visualizing the susceptibility distribution $\chi(\boldsymbol{x})$ in the region of interests (ROI) $\Omega$ which occupies the water and brain tissues.

nodes.name: Local field
nodes.statement: The first three steps extract the local field $b_l$ that is contained in the total field $b$: the offset correction removes/corrects $\theta_0(\boldsymbol{x})$ from $\theta(\boldsymbol{x})$ to obtain $b(\boldsymbol{x})\omega_0B_0TE$ (the offset corrected phase) lying in $(-\pi,\pi]$; the phase unwrapping removes the artificial jumps in the offset corrected phase when estimating the total field $b$; the background field removal eliminates the field induced by the susceptibility outside $\Omega$ such as skulls and nasal cavity.
nodes.statement_short: The local field b_l is what offset correction, phase unwrapping and background removal extract from the total field b.

nodes.name: Dipole inversion
nodes.statement_short: Recover chi in Omega from b_l via the principal-value convolution with the dipole kernel d.

nodes.name: Dipole convolution relation for the local field
nodes.statement: b_l(\boldsymbol{x})=\mathrm{pv}\int_{\Omega}d(\boldsymbol{x}-{\boldsymbol y})\chi({\boldsymbol y})\mathrm{d}{\boldsymbol y},
nodes.label: QSM_Deconv

nodes.name: Dipole kernel in the frequency domain
nodes.statement:
In the frequency domain, \cref{QSM_Deconv} reads
\begin{align} {\mathscr F}(b_l)({\boldsymbol{\xi}})={\mathcal D}({\boldsymbol{\xi}}){\mathscr F}(\chi)({\boldsymbol{\xi}})=\left(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{\xi_3^2}{|{\boldsymbol{\xi}}|^2}\right){\mathscr F}(\chi)({\boldsymbol{\xi}})
\end{align}
where ${\mathcal D}={\mathscr F}(d)$ is the Fourier transform of $d$ and ${\mathcal D}(\0)=0$  by the definition of $\mathrm{pv}$ \cite{L.deRochefort2010,E.M.Haacke2015}.
nodes.origin_citation: de Rochefort et al. 2010; Haacke et al. 2015

nodes.name: Dipole relation in the frequency domain
nodes.statement: {\mathscr F}(b_l)({\boldsymbol{\xi}})={\mathcal D}({\boldsymbol{\xi}}){\mathscr F}(\chi)({\boldsymbol{\xi}})=\left(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{\xi_3^2}{|{\boldsymbol{\xi}}|^2}\right){\mathscr F}(\chi)({\boldsymbol{\xi}})
nodes.origin_citation: de Rochefort et al. 2010; Haacke et al. 2015
nodes.label: QSM_Fou

nodes.name: Ill-posedness of dipole inversion
nodes.statement: From \eqref{QSM_Fou}, it is easy to see that recovering the susceptibility distribution $\chi$ is ill-posed as ${\mathcal D}=0$ on the critical manifold $\Gamma_0=\left\{{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\in{\mathbb R}^3:\xi_1^2+\xi_2^2-2\xi_3^2=0\right\}$.
conclusions: recovering the susceptibility distribution $\chi$ is ill-posed as ${\mathcal D}=0$ on the critical manifold $\Gamma_0=\left\{{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\in{\mathbb R}^3:\xi_1^2+\xi_2^2-2\xi_3^2=0\right\}$
nodes.statement_short: Dipole inversion is ill-posed because the kernel D vanishes on the conic critical manifold Gamma_0.

nodes.name: Truncated K-space division (TKD)
nodes.statement:
One benchmark method, called the truncated K-space division (TKD) \cite{K.Shmueli2009}, finds the approximate solution to \cref{QSM_Fou} via:
\begin{align} \chi_{\hbar}={\mathscr F}^{-1}({\mathcal X}_{\hbar}),~~~\text{where}~~{\mathcal X}_{\hbar}({\boldsymbol{\xi}})=\frac{\mathrm{sign}({\mathcal D}({\boldsymbol{\xi}}))}{\max\left\{|{\mathcal D}({\boldsymbol{\xi}})|,\hbar\right\}}{\mathscr F}(b_l)({\boldsymbol{\xi}})




\end{align}
with a threshold level $\hbar>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Direct inversion dividing by D in k-space with |D| truncated below a threshold.

nodes.name: TKD solution
nodes.statement: \chi_{\hbar}={\mathscr F}^{-1}({\mathcal X}_{\hbar}),~~~\text{where}~~{\mathcal X}_{\hbar}({\boldsymbol{\xi}})=\frac{\mathrm{sign}({\mathcal D}({\boldsymbol{\xi}}))}{\max\left\{|{\mathcal D}({\boldsymbol{\xi}})|,\hbar\right\}}{\mathscr F}(b_l)({\boldsymbol{\xi}})
nodes.label: TKD

nodes.name: Tikhonov regularization for QSM
nodes.statement:
Another method recovers $\chi$ via solving the following Tikhonov regularization \cite{B.Kressler2010}:
\begin{align} \min_{\chi}~\frac{1}{2}\left\|A\chi-b_l\right\|_2^2+\varepsilon\left\|\chi\right\|_2^2
\end{align}
where $\varepsilon>0$ and $A$ denotes the forward operator that is obtained by discretizing the kernel ${\mathcal D}$.

nodes.name: Tikhonov regularization problem
nodes.statement: \min_{\chi}~\frac{1}{2}\left\|A\chi-b_l\right\|_2^2+\varepsilon\left\|\chi\right\|_2^2
nodes.label: Tikhonov

nodes.name: Regularization based QSM model
nodes.statement:
Mathematically, it is formulated as solving the minimization problem:
\begin{align} \min_{\chi}~F(b_l|\chi)+R(\chi),
\end{align}
where $F(b_l|\chi)$ denotes the data fidelity term and $R(\chi)$ is the regularization term which mostly promotes the sparse approximation of $\chi$ under some linear transformation such as total variation and wavelet frames.
nodes.origin_citation: Kee et al. 2017; Wang et al. 2013

nodes.name: General regularization model
nodes.statement: \min_{\chi}~F(b_l|\chi)+R(\chi),
nodes.origin_citation: Kee et al. 2017; Wang et al. 2013
nodes.label: Regularization

nodes.name: Integral and differential approaches
nodes.statement: According to the choices of $F(b_l|\chi)$, the regularization based methods can be classified into the \emph{integral approaches} and the \emph{differential approaches} \cite{Y.Kee2017}.

nodes.name: Differential operator P(D)
nodes.statement:
The differential approaches are based on the following partial differential equation (PDE)
\begin{align} -\Delta b_l(\boldsymbol{x})=P(D)\chi(\boldsymbol{x})=\left(-\frac{1}{3}\Delta+\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x_3^2}\right)\chi(\boldsymbol{x})~~~~~~~\boldsymbol{x}\in\Omega
\end{align}
which is derived from the Maxwell's equation \cite{E.M.Haacke1999,J.K.Seo2014}.
nodes.origin_citation: Haacke et al. 1999; Seo et al. 2014

Integral approach with SMV filter

nodes.label: IntegralSMV

nodes.statement: Whenever the data acquisition is based on the PDE \cref{QSM_PDE}, the measured local field data will be written as the superposition of $b_l$ in \cref{QSM_Deconv} and the ambiguity of $-\Delta$, which will be referred as the \emph{harmonic incompatibility}.

Since the MRI signal is generated by the microscopic field $\mathbf{B}_{\ell}(\boldsymbol{x})$ experienced by the spins of water protons \cite{Y.Kee2017}, we use the following Lorenz sphere correction model \cite{E.M.Haacke1999}:
\begin{align} \mathbf{B}_{\ell}(\boldsymbol{x})=\mathbf{B}(\boldsymbol{x})-\frac{2}{3}\mu_0{\mathbf M}(\boldsymbol{x})
\end{align}
to relate $\mathbf{B}(\boldsymbol{x})$ and $\mathbf{B}_{\ell}(\boldsymbol{x})$.

Then for a given susceptibility distribution $\chi$ (in ${\mathbb R}^3$), the general solution $b$ which is bounded everywhere in ${\mathbb R}^3$ is expressed as
\begin{align} b(\boldsymbol{x})=\int_{{\mathbb R}^3}\Phi(\boldsymbol{x}-{\boldsymbol y})\left(-\frac{1}{3}\Delta_{{\boldsymbol y}}+\frac{\partial^2}{\partial y_3^2}\right)\chi({\boldsymbol y})\mathrm{d}{\boldsymbol y}+b_0
\end{align}
where $b_0$ is some constant, and $\Phi(\boldsymbol{x})=1/\left(4\pi|\boldsymbol{x}|\right)$.
conclusions:

nodes.name: Wave type structure of P(D)
nodes.statement: Notice that $P(D)$ is a ``wave type'' differential operator (by considering $x_3$ as the time variable). Indeed, the proof of \cref{NonVanishingSurfMeas} tells us that if $P(D)\chi=0$ in $\Omega$, such $\chi$ has a wave type structure in $\Omega$ regardless of its regularity, whereas the susceptibility of human brain does not have such a wave type structure \cite{J.K.Choi2014}. Hence in QSM, it follows that $-\Delta v$ defined as \cref{DistLapIncompatibility} is a nonvanishing surface measure on $\partial\Omega$, i.e. $-\Delta v=0$ in ${\mathbb R}^3\setminus\partial\Omega$, but $-\Delta v\neq0$ on $\partial\Omega$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Characterization of Harmonic Incompatibility in Local Field Data
nodes.statement_short: P(D) is wave-type; brain susceptibility lacks wave structure, so -Laplacian v is a nonvanishing surface measure on the boundary.
nodes.label: RK222

nodes.name: Numerical illustration of the harmonic incompatibility
nodes.statement: We present \cref{IllustrateTh1,IllustrateTh1Axial,IllustrateTh1Brain,IllustrateTh1BrainAxial} to illustrate \cref{Th1} by using the Shepp-Logan phantom (\cref{IllustrateTh1,IllustrateTh1Axial}) and the brain phantom (\cref{IllustrateTh1Brain,IllustrateTh1BrainAxial}). Using the limited total field $b$ in \cref{LoganTotal,LoganTotalAx,BrainTotal,BrainTotalAx} which are derived from \cref{Forward1} by placing strong susceptibilities outside $\Omega$, we solve \cref{LBV} using multigrid (MG) based the finite difference method \cite{D.Zhou2014} to obtain the measured local field $b_l$ in \cref{LoganMeasLocal,LoganMeasLocalAx,BrainMeasLocal,BrainMeasLocalAx} which are used for the susceptibility reconstruction. We also display the true local field $\widetilde{b}_l$ obtained from \cref{TrueLocalField} in \cref{LoganTrueLocal,LoganTrueLocalAx,BrainTrueLocal,BrainTrueLocalAx} for the comparison with the measured $b_l$. Finally, $v=b_l-\widetilde{b}_l$ and $|-\Delta v|$ are displayed in \cref{LoganIncomp,LoganIncompAx,BrainIncomp,BrainIncompAx} and \cref{LoganAbsLv,LoganAbsLvAx,BrainAbsLv,BrainAbsLvAx} respectively for better illustrations.
nodes.section: 2.2 Characterization of Harmonic Incompatibility in Local Field Data
nodes.statement_short: Shepp-Logan and brain phantoms: measured vs true local field, incompatibility v and |Laplacian v| displayed.

nodes.name: Grid index set and discrete ROI
nodes.statement: Let ${\mathbb O}=\left\{0,\cdots,N_1-1\right\}\times\left\{0,\cdots,N_2-1\right\}\times\left\{0,\cdots,N_3-1\right\}$ denote the set of indices of $N_1\times N_2\times N_3$ grids, and let $\Omega\subseteq{\mathbb O}$ denote the set of indices corresponding to the ROI.

nodes.name: Discrete ROI boundary
nodes.statement: Denote $\partial\Omega$ to be the indices of the boundary of ROI $\Omega$.

nodes.name: Discrete image space
nodes.statement: Finally, the space of real valued functions defined on ${\mathbb O}$ is denoted as ${\mathcal I}_3\simeq{\mathbb R}^{N_1\times N_2\times N_3}$.

nodes.name: Discrete measured local field
nodes.statement: Let $b_l\in{\mathcal I}_3$ be the (noisy) measured local field data obtained from \cref{LBV}, which satisfies $b_l=0$ in ${\mathbb O}\setminus\Omega$.

nodes.name: Discrete forward model with harmonic incompatibility
nodes.statement_short: Measured local field = A chi + harmonic incompatibility v + noise eta, with A the discretized dipole operator.

nodes.name: Discrete harmonic incompatibility
nodes.statement:
We observe that in the discrete setting, \cref{DistLapIncompatibility} in \cref{Th1} can be understood as
\begin{align} {\mathscr L} v=0\quad\text{in}\quad{\mathbb O}\setminus\partial\Omega\quad\text{ and }\quad {\mathscr L} v\neq0\quad\text{on}\quad\partial\Omega
\end{align}
with the discrete Laplacian ${\mathscr L}$, as ${\mathscr L} v$ is supported on $\partial\Omega$.
conclusions:
\label{DiscreteHarmonicIncompatibility}
{\mathscr L} v=0\quad\text{in}\quad{\mathbb O}\setminus\partial\Omega\quad\text{ and }\quad {\mathscr L} v\neq0\quad\text{on}\quad\partial\Omega
nodes.statement_short: Discretely, the incompatibility has discrete Laplacian zero off the boundary and nonzero on it.

nodes.name: Discrete harmonic incompatibility
nodes.statement: {\mathscr L} v=0\quad\text{in}\quad{\mathbb O}\setminus\partial\Omega\quad\text{ and }\quad {\mathscr L} v\neq0\quad\text{on}\quad\partial\Omega
nodes.label: DiscreteHarmonicIncompatibility

nodes.name: HIRE model
nodes.statement_short: Jointly fit chi and v: weighted data fit + lambda||L v||_1 sparsity of incompatibility + isotropic wavelet frame l1 on chi.

nodes.name: Wavelet frame HIRE model
nodes.statement: \min_{\chi,v\in{\mathcal I}_3}~\frac{1}{2}\left\|A\chi+v-b_l\right\|_{\Sigma}^2+\lambda\left\|{\mathscr L} v\right\|_1+\left\|\gamma\cdot W\chi\right\|_{1,2}
nodes.label: WaveletFrameHIRE

nodes.name: Isotropic l1 norm of wavelet frame coefficients
Isotropic l1 norm of wavelet frame coefficients
nodes.statement: \left\|\gamma\cdot W\chi\right\|_{1,2}:=\sum_{{\boldsymbol k}\in{\mathbb O}}\sum_{l=0}^{L-1}\gamma_l[{\boldsymbol k}]\left(\sum_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in{\mathbb B}}\left|\left(W_{l,\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\chi\right)[{\boldsymbol k}]\right|^2\right)^{1/2}.
nodes.label: IsoTropicWaveletFrame

nodes.name: HIRE reduces to integral and differential approaches
nodes.statement_short: With v=0 HIRE is the integral approach; with v=b_l-A chi it is an l1-fidelity differential approach.
nodes.label: RK231

nodes.name: Effect of harmonic incompatibility on low frequencies
nodes.statement: Even though more rigorous theoretical analysis is needed, we can somehow explain the effect of harmonic incompatibility in this manner; since the standard arguments on the harmonic functions (e.g. \cite{Evans2010}) tell us that $v$ is smooth and satisfies the mean value property except on $\partial\Omega$, it has slow variations on this region. As a consequence, it mostly affects the low frequency components in $b_l$ compared to the noise which mainly affects the high frequency components. Together with the fact that the critical manifold $\Gamma_0$ forms a conic manifold in the frequency domain, the harmonic incompatibility $v$ in $b_l$ mainly leads to the loss of ${\mathscr F}(\chi)$ in low frequency components.
nodes.statement_short: Smooth harmonic v mainly corrupts low frequencies of b_l, leading to loss of low-frequency F(chi).

nodes.name: Splitting variables
nodes.statement: More precisely, let $d=W\chi$, $e={\mathscr L} v$, $f=A\chi$, and $g=v$.

nodes.name: Constrained reformulation of the HIRE model
Split Bregman algorithm for the HIRE model
nodes.statement_short: ADMM/split Bregman: alternately solve chi,v quadratic subproblems, shrink d,e, update f,g, then Bregman variables.
nodes.label: Algorithm1

nodes.name: Main iteration loop
Iteration body
nodes.statement_short: Update chi and v, then d, e, f, g, then Bregman variables p, q, r, s.

nodes.name: Update chi and v
nodes.statement_short: Solve quadratic chi and v subproblems

nodes.name: chi subproblem
nodes.statement: \chi^{k+1}&=\operatornamewithlimits{argmin}_{\chi}~\frac{\beta}{2}\|A\chi-f^k+r^k\|_2^2+\frac{\beta}{2}\|W\chi-d^k+p^k\|_2^2
nodes.label: chisubproblem

nodes.name: v subproblem
nodes.statement: v^{k+1}&=\operatornamewithlimits{argmin}_{v}~\frac{\beta}{2}\|v-g^k+s^k\|_2^2+\frac{\beta}{2}\|{\mathscr L} v-e^k+q^k\|_2^2
nodes.label: vsubproblem

nodes.name: Update d, e, f, g
nodes.statement_short: Solve shrinkage and fidelity subproblems

nodes.name: d subproblem
nodes.statement: d^{k+1}&=\operatornamewithlimits{argmin}_d~\left\|\gamma\cdot d\right\|_{1,2}+\frac{\beta}{2}\|d-W\chi^{k+1}-p^k\|_2^2
nodes.label: dsubproblem

nodes.name: e subproblem
nodes.statement: e^{k+1}&=\operatornamewithlimits{argmin}_e~\lambda\left\|e\right\|_1+\frac{\beta}{2}\|e-{\mathscr L} v^{k+1}-q^k\|_2^2
nodes.label: esubproblem

nodes.name: f subproblem
nodes.statement: f^{k+1}&=\operatornamewithlimits{argmin}_f~\frac{1}{2}\|f+g^k-b_l\|_{\Sigma}^2+\frac{\beta}{2}\|f-A\chi^{k+1}-r^k\|_2^2
nodes.label: fsubproblem

nodes.name: g subproblem
nodes.statement: g^{k+1}&=\operatornamewithlimits{argmin}_g~\frac{1}{2}\|g+f^{k+1}-b_l\|_{\Sigma}^2+\frac{\beta}{2}\|g-v^{k+1}-s^k\|_2^2
nodes.label: gsubproblem

nodes.name: Update p, q, r, s
nodes.statement_short: Bregman variable updates

nodes.name: q update
nodes.statement: q^{k+1}&=q^k+{\mathscr L} v^{k+1}-e^{k+1}
nodes.label: qsubproblem

nodes.name: Closed form subproblem solutions
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that each subproblem has a closed form solution.
conclusions: each subproblem has a closed form solution

nodes.name: Closed form chi and v updates
Closed form chi update
nodes.statement: \chi^{k+1}&=\big(A^TA+I\big)^{-1}\big[A^T(f^k-r^k)+W^T(d^k-p^k)\big]
nodes.label: chisubexplicit

nodes.name: Closed form v update
nodes.statement: v^{k+1}&=\big(I+{\mathscr L}^T{\mathscr L}\big)^{-1}\big[g^k-s^k+{\mathscr L}^T(e^k-q^k)\big].
nodes.label: vsubexplicit

nodes.name: Soft thresholding d and e updates
Closed form d update (isotropic soft thresholding)
nodes.statement: d^{k+1}&={\mathcal T}_{\gamma/\beta}\big(W\chi^{k+1}+p^k\big)
nodes.label: dsubexplicit

nodes.name: Closed form e update (soft thresholding)
nodes.statement: e^{k+1}&=\max\big(|{\mathscr L} v^{k+1}+q^k|-\lambda/\beta,0\big)\mathrm{sign}\big({\mathscr L} v^{k+1}+q^k\big).
nodes.label: esubexplicit

nodes.name: Isotropic soft thresholding
nodes.statement_short: Isotropic soft thresholding shrinks the joint magnitude across bands at each level, keeping the low-pass band.

nodes.name: Closed form f and g updates
Closed form f update
nodes.statement: f^{k+1}&=\big(\Sigma+\beta I\big)^{-1}\big[\Sigma(b_l-g^k)+\beta(A\chi^{k+1}+r^k)\big]
nodes.label: fsubexplicit

nodes.name: Closed form g update
nodes.statement: g^{k+1}&=\big(\Sigma+\beta I\big)^{-1}\big[\Sigma(b_l-f^{k+1})+\beta(v^{k+1}+s^k)\big]
nodes.label: gsubexplicit

nodes.name: Convergence of the split Bregman algorithm
nodes.statement: Note that, since our model \cref{WaveletFrameHIRE} is convex, it can be verified that \cref{Algorithm1} converges to the minimizer of \cref{WaveletFrameHIRE} by following the framework of \cite[Theorem 3.2.]{J.F.Cai2009/10}, whenever it has the unique global minimizer.
assumptions: it has the unique global minimizer

nodes.name: Frame-Int and Frame-Diff comparison models
Wavelet frame integral approach (Frame-Int)
nodes.statement: \min_{\chi\in{\mathcal I}_3}~\frac{1}{2}\left\|A\chi-b_l\right\|_{\Sigma}^2+\left\|\gamma\cdot W\chi\right\|_{1,2}
nodes.label: WaveletFrameIntegral

nodes.name: Wavelet frame differential approach (Frame-Diff)
nodes.statement: \min_{\chi\in{\mathcal I}_3}~\frac{1}{2}\left\|{\mathscr L} A\chi-{\mathscr L} b_l\right\|_{\Sigma}^2+\left\|\gamma\cdot W\chi\right\|_{1,2}
nodes.label: WaveletFrameDifferential

nodes.name: TGV-HIRE, TGV-Int and TGV-Diff
nodes.statement:
Moreover, in order to highlight the main focus of this paper-to propose a two system regularization model by identifying a harmonic incompatibility in the measured local field data, we also test the models by replacing $\left\|\gamma\cdot W\chi\right\|_{1,2}$ in \cref{WaveletFrameHIRE,WaveletFrameIntegral,WaveletFrameDifferential} into the following TGV term:

nodes.statement: We can see that both the Frame-HIRE and the TGV-HIRE consistently outperform the existing direct approaches, the integral approaches, and the differential approaches in both cases.

nodes.name: Quasi-affine system
nodes.genus: the collection of the dilations and the shifts of the elements in ${\boldsymbol \Psi}$

nodes.name: Quasi-affine system
nodes.statement: {\mathscr X}({\boldsymbol \Psi})=\left\{\psi_{\alpha,n,{\boldsymbol k}}:1\leq\alpha\leq r,~n\in{\mathbb Z},~{\boldsymbol k}\in{\mathbb Z}^d\right\},
nodes.label: QASystem

nodes.name: Quasi-affine framelet dilations and shifts
nodes.statement:
\psi_{\alpha,n,{\boldsymbol k}}=\left\{\begin{array}{cl}
2^{\frac{nd}{2}}\psi_{\alpha}(2^n\cdot-{\boldsymbol k})~~&~~n\geq 0;\vspace{0.125em}\\
2^{nd}\psi_{\alpha}(2^n\cdot-2^{n}{\boldsymbol k})~~&~~n<0.
\end{array}\right.
nodes.label: QAFramelet

nodes.name: Tight wavelet frame
nodes.statement:
We say that ${\mathscr X}({\boldsymbol \Psi})$ is a tight wavelet frame on $L_2({\mathbb R}^d)$ if we have
\begin{align} \left\|f\right\|_{L_2({\mathbb R}^d)}^2=\sum_{\alpha=1}^r\sum_{n\in{\mathbb Z}}\sum_{{\boldsymbol k}\in{\mathbb Z}^d}\left|\left\langle f,\psi_{\alpha,n,{\boldsymbol k}}\right\rangle\right|^2
\end{align}
for every $f\in L_2({\mathbb R}^d)$.

nodes.name: Tight frame identity
nodes.statement: \left\|f\right\|_{L_2({\mathbb R}^d)}^2=\sum_{\alpha=1}^r\sum_{n\in{\mathbb Z}}\sum_{{\boldsymbol k}\in{\mathbb Z}^d}\left|\left\langle f,\psi_{\alpha,n,{\boldsymbol k}}\right\rangle\right|^2
nodes.label: TightFrame

nodes.name: Framelet and canonical coefficient
nodes.statement: In this case, each $\psi_{\alpha}$ is called a (tight) framelet, and $\left\langle f,\psi_{\alpha,n,{\boldsymbol k}}\right\rangle$ is called the canonical coefficient of $f$.

nodes.name: Refinable function and refinement mask
Refinement equation
nodes.statement: \phi=2^d\sum_{{\boldsymbol k}\in{\mathbb Z}^d}q_0[{\boldsymbol k}]\phi(2\cdot-{\boldsymbol k}).
nodes.label: MRA-RF

nodes.name: MRA based framelet construction
MRA-based framelet construction
nodes.statement: \psi_{\alpha}=2^d\sum_{{\boldsymbol k}\in{\mathbb Z}^d}q_{\alpha}[{\boldsymbol k}]\phi(2\cdot-{\boldsymbol k}),~~~~~\alpha=1,\cdots,r.
nodes.label: MRA-Fra

nodes.name: High pass and low pass filters
nodes.statement: The sequences $q_1,\cdots,q_r$ are called wavelet frame mask or the high pass filters of the system, and the refinement mask $q_0$ is also called the low pass filter.

nodes.name: Unitary extension principle (UEP)
nodes.statement:
The unitary extension principle (UEP) of \cite{A.Ron1997} provides a general theory of the construction of MRA based tight wavelet frames. Briefly speaking, as long as $\left\{q_0,q_1,\cdots,q_r\right\}$ are compactly supported and their Fourier series $\widehat{q}_{\alpha}({\boldsymbol{\xi}})=\sum_{{\boldsymbol k}\in{\mathbb Z}^d}q_{\alpha}[{\boldsymbol k}]e^{-i{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\cdot{\boldsymbol k}}$ satisfy
\begin{align} \sum_{\alpha=0}^r\left|\widehat{q}_{\alpha}({\boldsymbol{\xi}})\right|^2=1~~~~\text{and}~~~~\sum_{\alpha=0}^r\widehat{q}_{\alpha}({\boldsymbol{\xi}})\overline{\widehat{q}_{\alpha}({\boldsymbol{\xi}}+\boldsymbol{\nu})}=0
\end{align}
for all $\boldsymbol{\nu}\in\left\{0,\pi\right\}^d\setminus\left\{\0\right\}$ and ${\boldsymbol{\xi}}\in[-\pi,\pi]^d$, the quasi-affine system ${\mathscr X}({\boldsymbol \Psi})$ with ${\boldsymbol \Psi}=\left\{\psi_1,\cdots,\psi_r\right\}$ defined by \cref{MRA-Fra} forms a tight frame of $L_2({\mathbb R}^d)$, and the filters $\left\{q_0,q_1,\cdots,q_r\right\}$ form a discrete tight frame on $\ell_2({\mathbb Z}^d)$ \cite{B.Dong2013}.
conclusions: the quasi-affine system ${\mathscr X}({\boldsymbol \Psi})$ with ${\boldsymbol \Psi}=\left\{\psi_1,\cdots,\psi_r\right\}$ defined by \cref{MRA-Fra} forms a tight frame of $L_2({\mathbb R}^d)$
the filters $\left\{q_0,q_1,\cdots,q_r\right\}$ form a discrete tight frame on $\ell_2({\mathbb Z}^d)$
nodes.statement_short: If the masks' Fourier series satisfy the UEP identities, the MRA framelets form a tight frame.

nodes.name: Unitary extension principle conditions
